explanation: Option A is correct because both foreign keys are mandatory, so neither row can be inserted first without referencing a row that does not yet exist. The UNIQUE constraints help enforce the one-to-one cardinality, but they do not solve the insertion-order problem. The real difficulty is the circular dependency between Account and Contact. Option B is false because foreign keys can reference primary keys. Option C is false because one-to-one relationships can be mapped with foreign keys plus uniqueness. Option D is unrelated to the immediate constraint cycle.

options.text: Each insert would violate a mandatory foreign key unless the other row already exists, so the two tables form a dependency cycle
MySQL cannot enforce foreign keys when both tables use primary keys
A one-to-one relationship cannot be represented with foreign keys at all
The problem is only that the foreign keys are not indexed

prompt:
A schema has:

`Account(account_id PK, primary_contact_id FK NOT NULL UNIQUE)`
`Contact(contact_id PK, account_id FK NOT NULL UNIQUE)`

Each account must have exactly one contact, and each contact must belong to exactly one account. A developer wants to insert a new account and its contact in separate statements without disabling constraints. What is the best explanation of why this is difficult?
